Episode 1

The Rice-Feeding Ceremony at the Zamindar's Mansion

This is a story from long ago.

Along the banks of a river, over a modest but well-known estate, ruled a zamindar named Rajchandra Roy. Though his estate was not vast, his reputation was considerable. His relationship with his subjects was a good one — anyone in trouble never hesitated to come stand at the gates of the mansion for help.

But Rajchandra's greatest joy was his only son — Shashanka.

Shashanka was just six months old.

And for his Annaprashan — the ceremony marking a baby's first taste of rice — the zamindar's mansion seemed to overflow with celebration.

Since morning, the ceremonial band had struck up outside the house.

Dhong dhong dhong...

The shehnai's melody filled the air on every side.

The main gate was decked with garlands of mango leaves, bouquets of flowers, and banana trees. A huge pandal stood in the courtyard — seating for guests on one side, and on the other, massive hearths for cooking.

The kitchen looked as though it were preparing to feed a small army.

Ghee bubbled in the pans. Somewhere, luchis were frying. Somewhere else, fish curry. Elsewhere, pulao.

And there was no counting the sweets — sandesh, rasgolla, laddu, kheer-kadam — all being made at once.

The head cook, Haripada Thakur, shouted through his sweat,

"Oi, Nitai! Add a bit more ghee to that big pan! And listen — cut the fish carefully. Not a single fish can go to waste today!"

Nitai called back from a distance,

"Thakur-moshai, all the fish are fine. It's just this one fish that's got me a little worried."

"Why?"

"That's not a fish — it's more like a crocodile's little brother!"

Haripada turned to look. Set in a corner of the kitchen was an enormous catla fish. The fish weighed close to eighteen kilograms.

He stared at it a moment, then said,

"This isn't a fish... it's a whole household!"

Laughter rippled through the kitchen.

The Enormous Catla

This catla had been specially brought from a great river far away. The zamindar's order had been clear —

"For the Annaprashan feast, I want a fish so grand that guests will go home telling stories about it."

So the fish had been brought to the kitchen that very morning. Haripada himself tied up his waistcloth and sat down to cut it, a few assistants standing around him.

Sharpening his knife, he said,

"Come on then — let's see what's inside you!"

Nitai joked,

"Thakur-moshai, what if there's another fish inside such a big one?"

"Then I'll cut that one too."

"And what if there's a fish inside that one?"

Haripada paused his knife.

"You be quiet. Or I'll cut you first!"

Laughter rose again. The cutting began.

Once... twice... and then suddenly—

Clank!

A strange sound rang out against the blade. Haripada stopped.

"What was that sound?"

Nitai said, "Hit a bone?"

Haripada shook his head.

"No. That's not the sound of bone."

He carefully cut into the fish's belly. Then his eyes went wide.

"Oh!"

"What happened?"

Haripada reached into the fish's belly and pulled something out. A small object lay in his palm. As sunlight caught it, it flashed and glittered.

A diamond ring!

Everyone Stunned

For a moment, the kitchen fell completely silent. Nitai stood gaping.

Someone said, "A ring, inside a fish's belly!"

Haripada said,

"I've cut countless fish in my life. Out of a fish's belly I've found small fry, I've found prawns... but a ring — never!"

Someone said, "It must be someone's lost ring."

Another said, "But how did it end up in a fish's belly?"

No one had an answer.

Within moments the news traveled from the kitchen to the courtyard. Then from the courtyard to the veranda. And soon after—

"A diamond ring came out of a fish's belly!"

The news spread through the entire mansion. Guests began crowding around too.

The Ring Before the Zamindar

Rajchandra Roy was seated at that moment, talking with his guests. A servant ran up and said,

"Zamindar-babu! Something astonishing has happened!"

Rajchandra laughed and said,

"There's no shortage of astonishing things today. What is it?"

"A ring was found inside a fish's belly."

"What did you say?"

"A diamond ring."

Rajchandra rose to his feet. Before long, the ring was brought and placed before him. He picked it up.

An extraordinarily beautiful ring. At its center, a large, clear diamond. Around it, delicate engravings.

But the strangest thing of all — on the inside of the band, a few tiny letters were etched. Rajchandra narrowed his eyes, trying to read them. He could make nothing out.

He looked toward Queen Hemangini. She, too, stared at the ring in wonder.

"This ring surely doesn't belong to any ordinary person."

"It doesn't seem so," Rajchandra agreed.

An elderly relative said,

"Perhaps, many years ago, some wealthy person's ring fell into the river. The fish must have swallowed it."

Another immediately asked,

"Then it's been in the fish's belly all this time?"

The old man began, "Well, that—" but he could say no more, because the explanation didn't sound very convincing to anyone.

Whose Ring Is It?

The zamindar took the ring in his hand again. The diamond glittered strangely. He had seen fine gems before, but this diamond's light seemed somehow different.

"The ring will stay with me for now," he said.

The Queen smiled gently.

"But it was found in front of so many people. If the real owner is ever found?"

"Then I will certainly return it."

He slipped the ring into his pocket, then turned back to his guests as though nothing had happened — for today was his son's Annaprashan, and on such a joyful day, he did not wish to let the thought of a mysterious ring spoil the celebration.

Evening fell. All the ceremonies of the Annaprashan came to an end. Guests took their leave, one by one. The music of the band faded. The lights dimmed. After the day's whirlwind of activity, the mansion slowly grew quiet.

Shashanka had fallen asleep. The Queen had retired to her chamber.

Rajchandra sat alone in his room. A lamp burned on the table. He took the ring out of his pocket. He gazed at it for a while.

Then, to himself, he murmured,

"A ring from inside a fish's belly... there must be some mystery in this."

He brought the ring close to his finger. Just then, a light breeze slipped in from outside and made the lamp's flame flicker. The diamond flashed once.

Rajchandra stared, astonished.

He did not know —

that this small ring was about to open the door to the strangest chapter of his life.

And on the other side of that door waited a mystery beyond anything he could have imagined.

Episode 2

The Ring's Strange Power

Night had grown late.

All around the zamindar's mansion lay silence. Somewhere far off, a jackal howled. The day's clamor from the Annaprashan already felt like some distant memory.

Rajchandra Roy sat alone in his room. Before him, lamplight. In his hand, that mysterious diamond ring.

He could not stop thinking about the ring found in the fish's belly. He looked again at the inside of the band. Tiny letters were engraved there, but in the lamp's dim light he couldn't make them out clearly.

To himself, he said,

"Such a beautiful ring... but where could it have come from?"

Curiosity would not let him rest. He slipped the ring onto the index finger of his right hand.

A Strange Turn of Events

At first, nothing happened. Rajchandra looked at the ring and gave a small laugh.

"Haripada Thakur was right after all. Just because something comes out of a fish's belly doesn't make it magic!"

He rose and walked to the mirror. Then—

In an instant, the smile vanished from his face.

There was no face in the mirror!

He looked down at his chest. No hands. No feet. His entire body seemed to have vanished! Only his clothes floated in the air.

Rajchandra cried out in fear,

"What is this!"

He reached up to touch his own face. He could feel it with his hand, but he couldn't see it with his eyes.

He quickly pulled the ring off.

His body reappeared at once.

He stood in silence for a while. Then he put the ring back on. Invisible again. He took it off. Visible again.

There was no doubt left now.

The ring could make a person invisible!

Rajchandra's First Test

Rajchandra went to the door. Wearing the ring, he opened it. The two guards standing watch outside couldn't see him at all.

One said to the other, "Is Zamindar-babu in his room?"

"He is — he just went in a little while ago."

Rajchandra stood right in front of them and smiled faintly. He waved his hand. The guards saw nothing.

That was when it struck him — this ring's power was truly unbelievable.

He hurried back to his room and pulled the ring off. Then he sat in silence for a long time. Whether such a power should be in any human's hands at all — that question weighed on his mind.

The Queen Arrives

Just then, there was a soft knock at the door.

"Rajchandra?"

The Queen's voice. Rajchandra quickly set the ring down on the table.

"Come in."

The Queen entered. Looking at her husband's face, she said,

"Still awake this late? What's happened?"

Rajchandra hesitated, then said,

"That ring I got today..."

The Queen glanced at the table.

"That one?"

"Yes. I was... testing it a little."

"What did you find?"

Before Rajchandra could answer, a servant appeared at the door outside. Rajchandra picked up the ring quite naturally.

But suddenly it struck him —

the ring's secret should not be told to anyone.

"It's nothing. Just an odd ring, so I was looking at it."

The Queen said nothing more. She knew her husband well. But she sensed that Rajchandra was hiding something.

The Next Night

The following night, Rajchandra decided to test the ring again. This time he shut the door before putting it on. Invisible again.

He walked from one corner of the room to the other. He couldn't see his own body, but he could feel everything clearly.

He went toward the window. Suddenly his eye fell on the door. Set into the door was an old pane of blue glass — part of the mansion's old design, fitted above the door to let in light.

Out of curiosity, Rajchandra stood in front of the glass. And that was when the astonishing thing happened.

Through the glass, a faint outline of him could be seen!

He was stunned. He stepped a little to the right. The outline moved right too. He stepped left. It moved left too.

"How strange!" he whispered.

He understood at once—

in ordinary light he was invisible, but through this blue glass, he could be seen!

The Queen Truly Sees Him

Just then the Queen came to stand outside his door again.

"Rajchandra?"

No answer. She was about to open the door when, glancing through the blue glass, she froze. She could clearly see — Rajchandra standing inside the room!

Astonished, she said,

"You're standing right there, yet when I open the door I can't see you — why?"

Rajchandra realized then that the Queen could see him. He said nothing.

The Queen opened the door and stepped inside.

"Rajchandra?"

No one there.

She looked all around.

"What is going on!"

She stepped back outside and looked through the blue glass again. Rajchandra appeared once more!

A little frightened now, the Queen said,

"I can see you clearly from right here!"

The invisible Rajchandra laughed.

"Because you're looking through the blue glass."

The Queen was startled.

"You're really here?"

"Yes."

"But I can't see you!"

"It's because of this ring."

The Queen understood — the mystery lay in the ring found inside the fish's belly.

Blue Light

"Is there any other way to see you?" the Queen asked.

Rajchandra thought for a moment. Then he lit an old blue-glass lamp in the room. The room filled with blue light.

And astonishingly — the Queen could now see her husband from right inside the room.

"So that's the rule," Rajchandra said.

The Queen said slowly,

"In ordinary light, you're invisible. But through blue glass, or in blue light, you can be seen."

Rajchandra nodded.

"Yes. And this will stay between the two of us."

"I won't tell a soul," the Queen said.

For a while, the two of them fell silent. Then the Queen smiled gently.

"May I say something?"

"What?"

"All this time, we've needed people to hunt down every thief in the estate. Now we can just put you to work!"

Rajchandra laughed.

"So you've turned me from a zamindar into a spy!"

"Not a spy," the Queen said. "A man who knows the truth of his own kingdom."

At her words, Rajchandra stopped laughing. He thought for a moment, then said,

"You're right."

He looked out the window. Far off lay the countless villages of his estate. Somewhere, a farmer's home. Somewhere, a marketplace. Somewhere, his officials' quarters.

Everything he had learned all this time, sitting in his court — was all of it true? Perhaps not.

Rajchandra looked at the ring. Then, slowly, he said,

"Starting tomorrow night, I will see for myself — what is truly happening in my kingdom."

The Queen looked at him and said,

"Be careful."

Rajchandra smiled faintly.

"No one will even see me."

"Still," the Queen said, "remember — becoming invisible is easy. But facing the truth while invisible is not."

Rajchandra said nothing. He simply looked at the ring.

He did not know —

that this ring would very soon show him such truths that many familiar faces across his own estate would never look quite the same again.

Episode 3

The Invisible Zamindar

The next night.

One by one, every light in the mansion had gone out. The guards stood at their posts. A deep silence lay over everything.

Rajchandra Roy sat in his room. On the table, the diamond ring. Beside it, a small lantern.

Queen Hemangini stood by the door.

"You remember everything?"

Rajchandra smiled.

"Put the ring on, tell no one where I'm going, and if I see trouble, not try to play the hero."

"That last part matters most," the Queen said.

Rajchandra slipped the ring onto his finger. In an instant, his body vanished.

The Queen lit the blue lamp and looked at him one last time.

"Come back."

The invisible Rajchandra's voice answered,

"Of course."

The door opened. Then closed. No one noticed when the zamindar had slipped out of the room.

First Destination

That night Rajchandra decided to go first to Shalbanpur, the farthest village on his estate.

Visiting during the day was difficult for him — the moment people saw the zamindar, crowds gathered, everyone eager to voice their troubles.

But tonight, he was invisible.

After riding some distance, he dismounted near the village. He thought to himself,

"If I bring the horse along, people may not see me, but they'll certainly see the horse!"

So he tied the horse to a tree and walked on foot toward the village.

In a Farmer's Courtyard

In front of a hut, a few farmers sat talking.

One said, "The paddy's good this year. But after paying the rent, will there be any rice left at home?"

Another said,

"They say Zamindar-babu has talked about lowering the rent."

The first sighed.

"Zamindar-babu says so, sure. But does the estate manager listen?"

Rajchandra froze.

The manager?

All this while, he had assumed his orders were being carried out properly.

The farmer went on,

"He took extra money from us last time too."

Rajchandra's face darkened. He said nothing, only thought to himself —

"I'll have to check the accounts tomorrow."

But There's Another Side Too

On another edge of the same village, he saw an elderly farmer lying ill. There was no food in his house.

A little later, a servant from the mansion arrived, set down a sack of rice, and said,

"Zamindar-babu says — until you're well again, no one will ask you for rent."

The old man said in a trembling voice,

"Give my blessings to the young master."

The servant left. Rajchandra stood in silence.

He understood — not every servant was bad. Some carried out his orders faithfully. Others used his name for their own gain.

To understand a person's true face, one must watch from behind — not from the front.

A Funny Scene at the Market

As the night wore on, Rajchandra headed toward the market. In front of one shop, two men were arguing.

"You overcharged me by a rupee!" one said.

"Why would I do that?" the shopkeeper said.

"Because I gave you two rupees!"

"You gave me one!"

"Two rupees!"

Rajchandra stood listening. Finally, the shopkeeper said in exasperation,

"Fine — if you really gave two rupees, where's the other one?"

The man fumbled through his pockets, fell silent for a moment, and said,

"That... that one, I actually haven't given yet!"

The shopkeeper sat down and put his head in his hands.

The invisible Rajchandra laughed so hard that both men jumped and looked around.

"Who laughed?"

No one answered. Frightened, both men shut up shop and left.

Laughing, Rajchandra said,

"There are some advantages to being invisible, after all!"

But an Unsettling Piece of News Came at the End of the Night

On his way back, Rajchandra stopped near an old outpost. Inside, a few men sat talking in low voices. He went and stood by the window.

One said,

"They say the zamindar is finding out everything now."

Another said,

"Impossible. Who would tell him?"

The first said,

"It doesn't matter where the news is coming from. What matters is — the questions he's been asking about last month's accounts are no ordinary questions."

A third said,

"Then be careful. Someone may be watching us."

Rajchandra's heart pounded.

Had someone realized his invisibility?

He moved closer. But before he could hear more, someone inside shut the window. Rajchandra could hear nothing further.

The Shadow of an Invisible Visitor

The next night, he went out again. Night after night, he continued moving through different corners of his estate this way.

Somewhere, he saw the suffering of his subjects. Somewhere, the honesty of his officials. Somewhere, news of smuggling. And elsewhere, he saw poor people being threatened in his own name, through false orders.

Every day when he returned, he told the Queen everything. But no one besides the Queen knew a thing.

One night the Queen said,

"The things you're finding out — no one in this mansion should know them."

"That's exactly the problem," Rajchandra said.

"Why?"

"The more I learn, the more people I have to suspect."

The Queen was quiet a moment, then said,

"Then be careful. Because you may be invisible — but your enemies are not."

Rajchandra smiled faintly.

"Worrying again?"

"Yes."

"I have the ring."

"The ring can hide you from sight," the Queen said. "But not from danger."

This time, Rajchandra did not smile.

Eyes from Another Kingdom

A few days later, two strangers arrived at an inn near the border of the estate. Their clothes looked like ordinary merchants'. But their eyes lacked a merchant's usual curiosity.

That night, behind a closed door, they talked.

"The reports are matching up," one said.

"You're certain?" the other asked.

"Yes. The zamindar is learning things that have no way of reaching him."

"So?"

The first man said slowly,

"My guess is, he has some object that lets him become invisible and see everything."

The second man startled.

"Invisible?"

"I'm not certain yet. But if it's true..."

He didn't finish the sentence. Both fell silent. Outside the window, the night lay dark.

And somewhere in that darkness, far away, the invisible Rajchandra stood. He hadn't heard a word of their conversation.

He didn't know —

that news of his secret ring had now crossed the borders of his own kingdom into another.

And right after this news, a new danger was about to begin.

Episode 4

The Shadow of the Spies

From that night on, an invisible shadow seemed to hover around the zamindar's mansion.

Rajchandra Roy, however, noticed nothing at all.

As before, he went out at night wearing the ring — sometimes to the village market, sometimes to the riverside ghat, sometimes to a distant outpost of the estate.

But he did not know — someone was following him.

The Beginning of Suspicion

The two spies who had come from another kingdom called themselves Madhab and Keshab.

Disguised as merchants, they had spent several days roaming different parts of the estate. Their purpose was singular — how was the zamindar learning all this news?

One evening, they sat in a tea shop.

"Today the zamindar gave another order that matches exactly with what happened last night," Madhab said.

"But who's giving him the information?" Keshab asked.

"No one."

"Then how?"

Madhab looked around and said quietly,

"I think he's seeing it all himself."

Keshab laughed.

"Can a zamindar go wandering everywhere in the dead of night?"

"A human can't," Madhab said.

Keshab's laughter stopped.

"You mean..."

"Yes. I think we need to find out how he becomes invisible."

A Mistake

That night Rajchandra had gone to a village storehouse. He'd heard that farmers' paddy was being bought up secretly at low prices there.

Invisible, he listened to everything. Two officials were talking over accounts.

"How does the zamindar find out everything?" one said.

"I don't know. But we'd better be careful," the other said.

Just then, a dry bamboo pole snapped beneath Rajchandra's foot.

Crack!

The two men jumped.

"Who's there?"

No one answered. One picked up a lantern and looked around. He saw nothing.

Rajchandra held his breath and stood still. The man saw nothing.

"Must be a cat."

He walked away. Rajchandra let out a breath of relief.

But he did not know — outside the storehouse, standing in the dark, another man had seen everything. It was Madhab.

The Spy's New Clue

The next day Madhab told Keshab,

"I saw it."

"What?"

"The storehouse door was shut. No one was inside. And yet, there was the sound of a bamboo pole snapping."

"Did you see anyone?" Keshab asked.

"No."

"Then?"

Madhab said slowly,

"That no one could be seen — that's exactly the problem."

This time, Keshab did not laugh.

News of the Ring

After several days of inquiry, they learned that on the day of the Annaprashan, a diamond ring had been found inside the belly of a huge catla fish.

Madhab's eyes lit up.

"Where is the ring now?"

"With the zamindar," Keshab said.

"Then it all fits."

"How?"

Madhab said,

"His behavior changed the moment he got that ring. And ever since, he's known things he has no business knowing."

"But how can we be sure the ring makes a person invisible?" Keshab said.

"We'll find out," Madhab answered.

The Matter of the Blue Glass

The spies began collecting information about the mansion's layout. They learned that an old pane of blue glass was set into the door of the zamindar's room.

"There must be a reason for that too," Madhab said.

"An old house can have blue glass for no particular reason," Keshab said.

Madhab shook his head.

"Maybe. But the more coincidences pile up, the more suspicion grows."

Watching the Queen

The spies realized that trailing the zamindar directly to learn the ring's secret would be difficult — no one knew when or where he might appear.

So they chose a different path.

Queen Hemangini.

They began watching her.

One evening the Queen was walking in the garden. From behind the trees at a distance, Madhab watched her.

The Queen suddenly stopped. Somehow, she felt someone was watching her. She looked around. No one there.

But her eyes settled on a tree at the far end of the garden. Madhab stood silently behind it at that very moment.

The Queen watched a while longer, then walked away.

Madhab whispered,

"She suspects something."

Rajchandra's Mistaken Assumption

That night, Rajchandra was about to head out wearing the ring.

"Don't go today," the Queen said.

"Why?"

"Something doesn't feel right."

Rajchandra laughed.

"You're worrying without cause."

"I don't know why, but it feels like someone's watching us."

Rajchandra fell silent for a moment. Then he said,

"I stay invisible. No one can see me."

"They may not see you," the Queen said, "but they can still find your secret."

The words struck a chord in Rajchandra. Still, he went out that day.

A Terrible Plan

The next night, deep into the dark, Madhab and Keshab sat in an isolated room.

"If the ring is truly with the zamindar, getting hold of it is vital for us," Keshab said.

"Capturing the zamindar himself won't be easy," Madhab said.

"Then?"

Madhab said slowly,

"We take the one he trusts most."

Keshab understood at once.

"The Queen?"

Madhab nodded.

"Yes."

Keshab thought for a moment, then said,

"Then the zamindar will bring the ring to us himself."

A cunning smile crossed Madhab's lips.

"Exactly."

That very night, a few shadowy figures crept silently toward the outside of the zamindar's mansion in the darkness.

No one knew who they were. The guards noticed nothing at all.

And the zamindar sat in his room at that moment, gazing at the ring. The Queen was asleep in the next room.

Holding the ring in his hand, Rajchandra thought—

"This ring has shown me so much truth. But is my own family now in danger because of that truth?"

He did not know —

that the following dawn, upon waking, the most terrifying news of his life would be waiting for him.

The Queen was gone.

Episode 5

The Queen Held Captive

The first light of dawn had just touched the windows of the zamindar's mansion.

Rajchandra Roy's sleep broke to an unusual commotion outside the palace. He had barely sat up when there came a violent knocking at the door.

"Zamindar-babu!"

A guard's trembling voice outside. Rajchandra opened the door. Gasping, the guard said,

"A great disaster has happened!"

"What's happened?"

The guard lowered his head.

"The Queen... the Queen can't be found anywhere."

Rajchandra's face went pale in an instant.

"What are you saying?"

"At dawn, her maid went into her chamber and found the door open. The bed empty. A piece of cloth lying by the window."

Rajchandra ran to the Queen's room. The room wasn't in disarray. There was no sign of forced entry. Only, by the window, lay a torn piece of the Queen's scarf.

Rajchandra picked it up. An unknown dread settled deep in his chest.

A Letter

Just then, his eye fell on a small piece of paper lying on the table. He unfolded it. Only a few lines were written—

"The Queen is safe with us. If you want her back alive, come to the old river ghat before sunset today, bringing the diamond ring. Come alone."

There was no name below.

Rajchandra crushed the paper in his fist.

"The spies..."

Now all his earlier suspicions became clear at once. They had learned about the ring.

A Message for the Queen

Meanwhile, on the far side of the river, in an old abandoned house, Queen Hemangini sat captive. Her hands were not bound. But two guards stood outside the door.

The Queen sat calmly. One of the spies came in and said,

"Your husband will surely bring the ring."

"What will you do with the ring?" the Queen said.

"That's not for you to know."

"Do you even know that whoever wears this ring can become invisible?"

The spy paused for a moment. The Queen understood — they did not fully know the ring's power.

"Then what will you do once you have it?"

Irritated, the man said,

"Be quiet."

The Queen smiled softly.

"You're chasing after something whose true secret you don't even know."

The spy said nothing further.

Preparations at the Mansion

Alone in his room, Rajchandra sat staring at the ring. The Queen had always told him —

"Becoming invisible is easy. But carrying the weight of an invisible power is hard."

Today those words kept coming back to him.

He rose to go out with the ring. Then it struck him—

The blue glass.

If he became invisible with the ring on, ordinary people wouldn't see him. But through the blue glass, his presence might be revealed.

What if the spies somehow knew this rule too? Doubt crept into Rajchandra's mind. He decided he could not take any risks this time.

A Small Trick

Rajchandra called for his trusted old servant, Gadadhar.

"I'll be out for a while today. If anyone asks, tell them I've gone to the outpost on the northern side of the estate."

Gadadhar said, astonished,

"But you—"

Rajchandra raised a hand to stop him.

"Ask nothing more."

Gadadhar understood that something serious had happened. But he asked no further questions.

The Old River Ghat

As evening approached, the sky filled with clouds. The old river ghat had not been used in a long time. Tall trees stood all around. Broken steps led down into the water.

The place seemed to have been waiting a long time for some secret event.

Rajchandra saw the ghat from a distance. Then he slid the ring onto his finger. In an instant, he was invisible.

He moved slowly toward the ghat. But strangely, there was no one there. He looked all around.

Just then, a voice came from behind him—

"You've come right on time, Zamindar-babu."

Rajchandra stopped. The voice was coming from behind the trees on the far bank.

"Where is the Queen?"

"She is well."

"Bring her before me."

"The ring first."

Rajchandra stayed silent. The man stepped out from behind the trees. In his hand was a small piece of blue cloth. He said,

"We know you're invisible. But we also know you would never put your wife in danger."

Rajchandra's fist clenched.

"Give us the ring. Then take the Queen and go."

"And if I don't?"

The man gestured toward the far side of the river. A small boat came into view. The Queen sat inside it.

Rajchandra's heart trembled. The Queen could not see him either. But somehow, she seemed to sense her husband was near.

Lifting her head, she called out,

"Rajchandra, be careful!"

Rajchandra started to speak. But he stopped himself. This was no time to act on emotion.

The Final Test

"If you don't hand over the ring in the next moment, the boat goes to the middle of the river," the spy said.

Rajchandra looked toward the river. Then at his own finger. The diamond ring glinted even in the darkness.

On one side, the secret power he'd carried so long. On the other, the person dearest to his life.

Slowly, he slid the ring off his finger.

The spy's eyes lit up with joy.

"Now hand it to me."

Rajchandra closed his fist around the ring. Then, looking toward the river, he said, in a very calm voice—

"You wanted the ring."

"Yes."

"But you don't know the difference between owning a ring — and being its slave."

The spy frowned. Rajchandra took one step toward the river.

What would he do in the next moment?

The spies did not know. The Queen did not know. Only Rajchandra knew—

that this very night, the fate of the diamond ring was about to change forever.

To be continued...
↑ Back to Table of Contents
Episode 6 · Final

The Diamond Ring in the River

Evening had fallen along the riverbank.

The last light of the sky was slowly fading. Dark clouds gathered in the west. In the darkness, the river's water looked deeper, and stranger, than ever.

Rajchandra Roy stood by the river. He was invisible. In his fist, the diamond ring. And on the far side of the river, in a boat, sat the captive Queen Hemangini.

The spies' leader shouted again,

"Hand the ring over to us!"

Rajchandra said nothing. He simply looked out at the river.

Because of this ring, over the past few weeks, he had wandered every corner of his kingdom, invisible. He had seen people's true faces. He had seen injustice; he had seen love; he had seen betrayal.

And because of this same ring, his Queen was captive today.

He remembered the Queen's words—

"Becoming invisible is easy. But carrying the weight of an invisible power is hard."

Suddenly, the Queen's voice carried from the boat,

"Rajchandra!"

He startled. The Queen couldn't see him, yet somehow she seemed to know her husband was near.

"Don't give up the ring for me!"

The spy snapped angrily,

"Quiet!"

The Queen spoke again, calmly this time.

"If you hand over the ring, they could put both of us in danger. Do what you believe is right."

Rajchandra's chest tightened. He understood — the Queen trusted his decision completely.

The Spies' Final Warning

The spies' leader stepped forward along the bank.

"I'll say it one last time. Hand over the ring."

Slowly, Rajchandra opened his fist. In the moonlight, the diamond flashed. The spies' eyes fixed on the ring.

"Yes... now come closer."

Rajchandra took the ring in his hand and stepped forward. Then another step.

The spies' leader held out his hand.

"Give it here."

Rajchandra smiled and said,

"Did you really think I'd hand this over to you?"

The spy was stunned.

"What did you say?"

"You can take away my power to become invisible. But you cannot take away my decision."

The spy shouted,

"Give me the ring!"

Rajchandra turned toward the river.

A Single Moment

The river's current ran strong and deep. Rajchandra looked at the ring one last time.

The diamond's glimmer seemed to bring back many days of memory.

That first day — the joy of the Annaprashan. The enormous catla fish. The ring emerging from its belly.

Then, becoming invisible himself. The Queen's astonished face. Being seen through the blue glass. His body becoming visible again in blue light.

Then, countless nights. Wandering alone down dark paths. Watching people's joys and sorrows.

This ring had given him a kind of sight no ordinary person possessed.

But today, he understood—

Keeping the person he loved safe mattered more than any power to see everything.

Softly, he said,

"Farewell."

Then—

He hurled the ring into the deep water of the river.

Rajchandra throws the diamond ring into the river — Episode 6

Splash!

A small sound. And then, nothing more. The diamond ring vanished into the dark bosom of the river.

The Spies' Despair

"No!"

The spies' leader ran wildly toward the river. He waded into the water searching for the ring. His companions waded in too.

One dove under. Another felt along the riverbed with his hands. But the river flowed on at its own pace. There was no trace of the ring.

The spies' leader screamed in rage,

"What have you done!"

Rajchandra said calmly,

"A thing that stirs up greed and malice in people — it's better that it doesn't exist in this world."

The spy started toward him, then stopped short — because Rajchandra was still invisible. He had no idea where he was.

The Queen's Release

Realizing the ring was gone, the spies' plan fell apart. There was no longer any point in keeping the Queen captive.

A little later, she was brought down from the boat.

The moment the Queen's feet touched the ghat, Rajchandra moved toward her. He was still invisible.

Looking around, the Queen smiled softly.

"Are you still here?"

"Yes."

"The ring?"

Rajchandra looked toward the river.

"Gone."

The Queen was silent for a moment. Then she said,

"Does it hurt very much?"

Rajchandra sighed.

"It does. It feels like I've thrown away some strange power with my own hands."

"You haven't lost a power," the Queen said.

"Then what?"

"You've proven your mastery over it."

Rajchandra said nothing. The Queen spoke again.

"Come, let's go home."

The Last Blue Light

That very night, they returned to the mansion.

Rajchandra stepped into his room and stood still. The ring was gone. And yet, he remained invisible.

The Queen lit the old blue lamp in the room. In the blue light, Rajchandra's form slowly grew clear.

The Queen looked at him and smiled gently.

"Today's the last time I'll see you like this, in this blue light."

"Maybe that's for the best," Rajchandra said.

"Why?"

"Because from now on, I won't need to be invisible to know the truth."

The Queen looked at him, surprised.

"I'll go to the people myself. I'll listen to them. I'll see with my own eyes. And if any official of mine does wrong, I'll see that he's punished."

"So the ring left you with a lesson after all," the Queen said.

"What lesson?"

The Queen smiled softly.

"Eyes are enough to see people. But it takes a heart to understand them."

Rajchandra smiled too.

Many Years Later... 🌊

Years passed.

The events of that Annaprashan slowly turned into a tale told by word of mouth.

Some said the ring found in the fish's belly had been cursed. Others said it was some royal family's lost treasure. Still others said the ring lay in the riverbed even now.

But the truth was known to only two people — Rajchandra Roy and Queen Hemangini.

And the river? The river knew everything.

Many monsoons came and went after that night; the river rose and fell, again and again.

But somewhere deep within it, the mysterious diamond ring remained hidden.

A ring that could make a person invisible.

But in the end, that very ring had taught someone —

Power lets you see everyone. But only love lets you truly see a person.

💎 THE END 🌊
